column1: Join us for a fun, step-by-step canvas class featuring an adorable spooky-season Highland cow.

No painting experience is needed—we’ll guide you through the entire project and help you create a canvas you’ll be excited to pull out every Halloween. Bring a friend, make it a girls’ night or date night, and enjoy a creative evening with just the right mix of cute, creepy, and cozy fall vibes.

We are excited to offer a selection of alcoholic beverages!  Your first beverage of the evening is included with your booking, and another can be purchased at the event!  Choose from a variety of local wines, ice cold beers, ciders, and seltzers! We have something for everyone. If you would rather skip the liquor, we also have sodas, coffee, and water available for you! A snack is also included in your reservation fee, but feel free to bring in your favorite food to munch on while you paint!

These tickets are not transferable, and the deposit is not refundable but does apply to your ticket that evening.  Your fee can be applied to a different class if you cannot attend this one or gifted to a friend if you let us know that you would like to do that in advance.  Our number is (970) 243-0886.  Do not purchase tickets from strangers on the internet.

column1: Messy Hands Art Club is a hands-on homeschool art class designed for curious, creative students ages 7–12 who love to make (and don’t mind getting a little messy along the way!). Held in our studio, this class invites young artists to explore, experiment, and build skills in a relaxed and encouraging environment.

Over the course of the program, students will work with a variety of art mediums—including watercolor, acrylic paint, clay, and more—while learning techniques, creative problem-solving, and artistic confidence. Each session offers a new project and plenty of room for self-expression.
Classes are taught by Kat Scarborough, a certified K–12 art instructor and focus on process over perfection—because the best learning happens when hands are busy and imaginations are wide open.
All supplies are included—just bring your creativity and a willingness to get your hands messy!
Deposits are non-refundable but may be applied to another class if cancellation occurs with more than 24 hours notice.

Join us for the October meeting of our Pottery Studio Book Club!
No assigned reading, no pressure — just good conversation, wine, and creativity. Bring a book you’ve read recently and loved (it can be one you’re currently reading or something you finished earlier this year). We’ll each share what’s been lighting up our bookshelves, sip a glass of wine, and make something beautiful together.

column1:

Choose one of preselected vinyl designs, and we will press it onto a book bag for you and we will paint them the night of the class!

In March 2023, a year after Russia invaded Ukraine, Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich met with a source in an empty restaurant 900 miles east of Moscow. Masked agents charged in, blindfolded Gershkovich, and dragged him into an unmarked van. The agents were from the FSB, Putin’s security service, and the successor to the Soviet-era KGB. Five years earlier, Gershkovich—whose parents had left the Soviet Union in the 1970s for New Jersey—arrived in Moscow to start his journalism career.

column1: Interrogated for hours after his arrest, Gershkovich was charged with spying and thrown in Moscow’s notorious Lefortovo prison—a pawn in a geopolitical chess match. After his world shrunk to a tiny cell, Gershkovich continued reporting. For the next sixteen months, he documented a life in Russia that few Westerners will ever experience: its sprawling prison system, with its own vocabulary and customs—and surprising pockets of humanity.

In This Cursed Beautiful Land: A Russian-American Story, Gershkovich recounts the events leading to his arrest, his nearly 500 days in Russian prisons, and the multi-country prisoner swap that freed him. More than a prison memoir, it’s a chronicle of a misunderstood people and their land.
Gershkovich will be in conversation with Peter Baker, the chief White House correspondent for The New York Times.

This event will be ASL-interpreted. To sit in the interpreted section or to access the interpreted feed virtually, contact Amanda.

column1: 6:30 pm: Happy Hour

Simchat Torah, which means “Rejoicing in Torah,” is the day when we gather to renew ourselves as we begin the cycle of reading from Genesis once again. Let loose and dance like no one’s watching as you enjoy live music, themed cocktails and mocktails, and lively dancing on I Street.
Before the main event, choose from taking a class with Rabbi Jenna diving into the holiday and exploring the first few lines of the Torah, or get social and meet new people at our happy hour.

On Simchat Torah, we read the very first lines of Torah and the story of creation – not making something out of nothing but rather creating order out of chaos – tohu va-vohu. In a world that at times feels too chaotic to comprehend, how can we continue to create meaningful and joyful experiences? Explore these big questions and more through a text study with Rabbi Jenna.

Must be 21+ and present ID to attend. No one will be turned away from any of our programs due to lack of funds. For more information, please contact our Director of Jewish Life,  Nathan.

From his fractured childhood through recounting his career through twelve of his most iconic films, Academy Award, Golden Globe, and Emmy Award-winning actor and producer Michael Douglas finally gives the full and uncensored account of his life in One Helluva Ride.

column1: Initially dismissed as just the handsome son of legendary movie star Kirk Douglas, at age thirty-one Douglas surprised Hollywood when he won his first Oscar for producing One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. Told he would never be more than a TV actor, he quit the hit series “The Streets of San Francisco” and went on to win a second Oscar for his performance in Wall Street.
Yet as Douglas’s fame grew, so did his personal struggles: his turbulent first mar­riage
column3: his struggle with alcohol, drugs and rehab
column4: the fight to save his son from an addiction that sent him to prison
column5: and his battle with stage IV cancer. He saw Catherine Zeta Jones on a movie screen and instantly fell for her. Their incredible love story transformed his life, enduring after twenty-five years of marriage.

column1:
Douglas will be in conversation with Kelly Corrigan, the author of four New York Times bestselling memoirs about family life as well as two children’s books. She hosts the podcast, “Kelly Corrigan Wonders,” and the show “Tell Me More” on PBS.

Eight years after redefining “flavor without fuss,” Yotam Ottolenghi—one of the most influential voices in contemporary food—offers Simple Too, the follow-up to his bestselling cookbook, Ottolenghi Simple. In a world of endless notifications, Ottolenghi explores what “simple” means now and why bold flavor remains at the heart of simplicity. In conversation, he’ll share recipes that work with you, not against you, and dishes you can begin with half a plan and still end with a deeply satisfying meal.

column1: Ottolenghi will dive into the ingredients and techniques that shape this new collection: beans simply dressed, black chickpeas, sesame in generous handfuls, sweet-and-spicy balances, pasta cooked directly in its sauce, and whole meals roasted in a single tray. He’ll also introduce the “Fundamentals” chapter—fifteen fridge-ready flavor builders like spring onion oil, green salsa, za’atar oil, confit tomatoes, and chilli crisp—small things that make big differences on busy weeknights. Simple Too is less about doing less and more about making everyday cooking feel generous, achievable, and full of joy.

Renowned for his vegetable-forward cuisine and imaginative approach to everyday cooking, Ottolenghi’s acclaimed cookbooks include Plenty, Jerusalem, Simple, Flavor, and Sweet. His work extends to successful delis and restaurants, where bold combinations, fresh produce, and multicultural inspirations meet. Ottolenghi will be in conversation with Carla Hall, a chef, co-host of the YouTube show “Chewed Up,” former co-host of the Emmy Award-winning TV show “The Chew,” and the author most recently of Carla Bakes: Sweet, Savory, and from the Heart.

This service will be ASL-interpreted. To sit in the interpreted section or to access the interpreted feed virtually, contact Amanda.

Listen to Chelsea Wolfe

column1: Acclaimed musician, songwriter, and multidisciplinary artist Chelsea Wolfe returns with new music at the center of a world that she is only beginning to reveal. “The Dark” and “Death is Not the End” arrive after a week of fan speculation, sparked by cryptic imagery, fragments of sound, and the shadowy visual language teased by Heretic Parfum across its socials.

Wolfe has become one of the most singular artists in the world, moving fluidly between doom metal, folk, industrial, electronic music, and spectral balladry. She has collaborated with artists including Deftones’ Chino Moreno, Xiu Xiu, and Converge, had her music featured in HBO’s “
column3: co-wrote the score for the A24 horror film X with Tyler Bates, and turned heads at last year’s Ann Demeulemeester show at Paris Fashion Week.

column1: Known for building immersive worlds where darkness and beauty are indistinguishable, Wolfe has cultivated a devoted global following through music that explores transformation, spirituality, grief, longing, and the unseen forces that shape our lives. With these new songs and GHOSTS arriving in close succession, she opens the door to a new chapter that feels unmistakably her own.

Listen to Simone Dinnerstein

column1: Lauded by The Washington Post as “an artist of strikingly original ideas and irrefutable integrity,” Simone Dinnerstein returns for an evening of distinctive artistry. The program opens with Rameau’s rarely performed Gavotte et six doubles, followed by American composer Philip Lasser’s Twelve Variations on Chorale by J.S. Bach, exploring the power and modernity of Bach’s harmonic poetry. Dinnerstein continues to demonstrate her “unique voice in the forest of Bach interpretation” (The New York Times) with the composer’s 15 Sinfonias, and closes her program with Keith Jarrett’s Encore from “Tokyo,” ending the night on a note of otherworldly serenity.
column3: :0,&quot

column1: Dinnerstein’s performance is the fifth-annual Ruth Bader Ginsburg Memorial Recital—a creative initiative connecting Justice Ginsburg’s love of music, the esteemed artists she championed and befriended, and the future of the vocal and instrumental arts in which she delighted.

Agnelo Fernandes, keys

Celebrated sitar maestro Niladri Kumaar is a compelling force in Indian classical music and an innovator who carries centuries of tradition in every note. This evening is both a forward-looking showcase and a tribute to an irreplaceable musical bond: curated selections from Space Between the Notes, the only recorded live performance between Kumaar and the late, legendary Zakir Hussain. Their singular partnership resounds once more—a gift, before the album’s release later this year.

Featuring sitar, zitar, and an ensemble of Indian and American musicians with jazz influences, this is Indian music at its most expansive, where centuries of classical tradition meet improvisational spirit.

Sophia Bush has always understood the power of stories. She’s seen it in the connection millions of viewers have had to the women she’s played on-screen—Dr. Sam Griffith on “Good Sam” and Dr. Cass Beckman on “Grey’s Anatomy,” Detective Erin Lindsay on “Chicago P.D.,” and the iconic Brooke Davis on “One Tree Hill.” She’s seen it in her activism, where speaking truth to inequality and power has prompted real change. And she’s seen it in her personal life, when her experiences and opinions have been distorted to drive clicks and create drama.

column1: In And I Will Tell You Mine, Bush shares stories about what has most shaped her: her childhood in Los Angeles, the unexpected road from journalism student to actor, navigating Hollywood and fighting for her character’s integrity, and the realities of marriage and divorce. She also offers sides of herself not often seen: the lifelong learner, the friend, the adventurer. And I Will Tell You Mine is an account of becoming, un-becoming, and becoming again to return home to our truest selves.

This service will be ASL-interpreted. To sit in the interpreted section or to access the interpreted feed virtually, contact Amanda.

In the 1970s, the ultimate trip for any backpacker was the storied “Hippie Trail,” a 3,000-mile trek from Istanbul to Kathmandu. A 23-year-old Rick Steves made the trek in 1978, and like a travel writer in training, he documented everything along the way: jumping off a moving train, making friends in Tehran, getting lost in Lahore, getting high for the first time in Herat, battling leeches in Pokhara, and more. The experience ignited his love of travel and forever broadened his perspective on the world.

Fire –

column1: Air –
column2: the element of motion, freedom, self-awareness, and skillfulness &#8211
column3: guides you as you move forward and take flight.

column1: Earth –
column2: the element of stability, self-care, steadiness, and nourishment &#8211
column3: is all about training. You need to continue the work so change can be lasting.

column1: Water –
column2: the element of letting go, generosity, and adaptability &#8211
column3:

column1: “A genuine artist, with a thoughtfully conceived and poetic interpretation.” – The New York Times

Pianist Minsoo Sohn debuts with Washington Performing Arts for a program exhibiting his undeniable musical intelligence and masterful virtuosity. Studied by the likes of Beethoven and Mozart, Bach’s The Well-Tempered Clavier, Book I, is frequently regarded as one of the most significant works in the history of classical music. Sohn brings his own poetic interpretation to this storied collection of 24 prelude and fugue pairs, creating an unforgettable evening with one of the most audacious and influential works for piano as the centerpiece.
Known for his career as a devoted pedagogue, Sohn is also recognized as the teacher of Yunchan Lim, the youngest first-prize winner in the history of the Van Cliburn International Piano Competition.

Listen to the Aga Khan Master Musicians

column1: Aga Khan Master Musicians
Basel Rajoub, saxophone and clarinet
Feras Charestan, qanun
Yurdal Tokcan, oud
Abbos Kosimov, drum
Vincent Peirani, accordion

Washington Performing Arts presents an evening where the musical worlds of Central Asia, China, the Middle East, and contemporary Europe meet in striking and unexpected harmony. Five performers from the Aga Khan Master Musicians—an artistic collective dedicated to living musical traditions—are joined by celebrated French artist Vincent Peirani for a concert that is wholly its own.
Syrian-born Basel Rajoub has reimagined an entirely new vocabulary for the saxophone
column2: his compatriot Feras Charestan commands the qanun, the shimmering Middle Eastern plucked zither. Turkish oud master Yurdal Tokcan and Uzbek percussionist Abbos Kosimov, a virtuoso on the doira frame drum, complete the collective’s lineup. They are joined by Vincent Peirani, award-winning accordionist, singer, and composer whose work spans jazz, contemporary music, and improvisation. Six distinct voices in one extraordinary evening.

Listen to Haley Heynderickx

column1: Following the release of her acclaimed debut I Need to Start a Garden and its long-awaited follow-up Seed of a Seed, Haley Heynderickx recently released What of Our Nature, a collaboration with Max García Conover. After a year of touring with Garcia and working on new material, she now returns to the road for a rare run of solo performances.

One of contemporary folk’s most quietly captivating voices, Heynderickx writes with warmth, wit, and self-reflection. Her songs find wonder in the everyday while exploring questions of identity, belonging, and our relationship with the natural world. Tender, thoughtful and quietly spellbinding, these shows are an invitation to step into the unknown with her and leave a little room for what may come next.

Listen to Seth Parker Woods

column1: Listen to Conor Hanick

Cellist Seth Parker Woods and pianist Conor Hanick unite for an evening of commanding musicianship at the intersection of tradition and discovery. A three-time GRAMMY nominee, Woods has garnered a reputation for versatile and inventive musicality, and is joined by pianist Hanick, praised for his precision with classic and contemporary fare.

Their program brings together Fazil Say’s vivid Four Cities, George Walker’s 1956 Sonata for cello and piano—of which Gramophone writes that Woods and Hanick’s recording is “more compellingly characterful,” with “the raw vulnerability of the central slow movement” lingering in the memory — and Rachmaninoff’s sweeping Cello Sonata, op. 19, one of the most passionate works in the duo repertoire.

Listen to the Balourdet Quartet

column1: Recipient of the 2024 Avery Fisher Career Grant and Chamber Music America’s Cleveland Quartet Award, the Balourdet Quartet was born from late-night chamber music sessions and became one of the most celebrated young ensembles in the world. Described as “unafraid to show its personality,” their playing balances clarity with expressive warmth, and a deep belief that music exists to break down walls. Their Washington Performing Arts program reflects that ambition: spanning four centuries from Monteverdi to Ben Johnston’s microtonal meditation on “Amazing Grace,” with Bartók’s haunted and personal Sixth Quartet, and Mendelssohn’s passionately constructed Second at the center.

Listen to Paul Huang

column1: Four acclaimed musicians join together in a powerful program meditating on time, loss, and hope. Bela Kovacs’ Sholem Alekhem, rov Feidman! is a vibrant clarinet homage to klezmer song and spirit, laughter edged with lament. It casts light on the echoes that follow, reminding us that even in the face of ruin, sound endures. Shostakovich’s Piano Trio No. 2, written amid war and loss, spins a ghostly klezmer dance: ironic, grief-stricken, unforgiving. Messiaen’s Quartet for the End of Time, born in a prison camp, reaches beyond suffering toward eternity, where time dissolves into silence and praise. These works are fragments of memory, breath, and belief
column2: resonating through the stillness that time leaves behind.

Based on the popular book by Victoria Kann and Elizabeth Kann, this is the tale of Pinkalicious, who can’t stop eating pink cupcakes despite warnings from her parents. Her pink indulgence lands her at the doctor’s office with Pinkititis, an affliction that turns her pink from head to toe—a dream come true for this pink-loving enthusiast. Alas, Pinkalicious needs a way out of her pink predicament, and joined by her family they find unity and appreciation in the quirks that define us all.

If you would like to book a slot for one of our field trip matinees, please contact Autumn (autumnmlct@gmail.com).

Trolls JR. is based on the irreverent DreamWorks Animation movie franchise and features a colorful, wondrous world populated by hilariously unforgettable characters. The show follows the overly optimistic Trolls, constantly with a song on their lips, and the comically pessimistic Bergens, who are only happy when they have Trolls in their stomach.

The Troll thespians in Poppy’s company live by their motto: the show must go on. But when a tyrannical foreign emissary arrives in Bergenland, expectations are raised, forcing the Trolls to totally rework their show or risk being served up in the name of diplomacy by a Chef rehired and out for revenge.

If you would like to book a slot for one of our field trip matinees, please contact Autumn (autumnmlct@gmail.com).
